name: Scientific blackpill

lead: The 'scientific blackpill' is a curated set of studies, such as on facial attractiveness and online dating, that proponents cite to argue appearance matters a great deal in dating. For looksmaxxers it is a motivation: if looks matter, improving them matters.

The broader blackpill worldview holds that attractiveness is largely fixed by genetics, which conflicts with looksmaxxing's premise that it can be improved. Researchers describe the citation style as selective, relying on single studies and favourable readings.

paras: In practice it means reading, collecting and sharing studies, often on forum wikis, and using them in discussions of which features or factors matter.

Scholars and advocacy groups link the wider blackpill outlook to fatalism and hostility, and say its use of science is selective. Readers are encouraged by researchers to look at studies in full rather than through curated lists.

angle.text: Some use the studies as justification for looksmaxxing. Proponents of the blackpill worldview instead conclude improvement is limited.

lead: The 'scientific blackpill' refers to collections of research on attractiveness, mate choice and dating-site behaviour that blackpill adherents use to support their view of the dating market. The incel community maintains a wiki page by this name.[1]

Blackpill ideology, as described in encyclopedic sources, is a fatalistic variant of the 'red pill' that holds dating success is set largely by genetics and status, so appearance improvement is futile.[2] In looksmaxxing spaces the same studies are often read the other way: if looks matter, improving them is worthwhile.

Scholars describe the style of argument critically. The Institute for Strategic Dialogue calls it argument by exhaustion, using many references of dubious quality to support weak claims, and critics note single studies and cherry-picking.[2] Evolutionary psychologists have disputed how incels read their field.[2]

paras: The framework draws on evolutionary psychology and dating-site studies, which adherents cite for claims such as the '80/20 rule' that most women prefer the top fifth of men.[2]

The Institute for Strategic Dialogue describes the appeal to science as argument by exhaustion.[2] Researchers William Costello and David Buss have suggested extreme inceldom resembles suicidality more than violence toward others, and the Anti-Defamation League and others have described the ideology as dangerous.[2]
No studies found on the 'scientific blackpill' as a collection. Individual attractiveness and dating studies exist in psychology, but are cited selectively according to critics.[2]
